newsitem.title: USA: Bruno sees narrow agenda for N.Y. special session.
newsitem.headline: Bruno sees narrow agenda for N.Y. special session.

text.p: The New York Senate Majority Leader predicted that the mid-December special legislative session likely will have a fairly narrow agenda, and postpone tackling tough issues like welfare reform until next year.
One of the main issues that the lawmakers are expected to address is improving New York City's school administration by giving the chancellor more authority.

But proposals on school governance and on budget reform, another key issue the special legislative session could tackle, have not yet been finalized, a spokesman for the Leader, Joseph Bruno (R-Troy), said on Wednesday.
While New York City had hoped that the special session also would take up its plan to create a new infrastructure authority, which is needed to sidestep the debt cap, this now does not appear likely.

"I think it would be very difficult for us to try to do that in a special session, so that's not on my horizon," Bruno told reporters in Albany on Tuesday. He explained that this was a complicated issue that would require considerable review.

The same holds true for the governor's welform reform bill. The Assembly is expected to oppose measures that go further than those needed to put the state's plan in compliance with the new federal law.
"I think that's going to be difficult to resolve in the next couple of weeks," Bruno said.

However, the Republican-led Senate and the Democrat-controlled Assembly are expected to address one of the city's more pressing concerns by extending a personal income tax surcharge that otherwise would expire at year-end.

And the Metropolitan Transportation Authority, which is expected to get about $500 million in fiscal 1997 from a 17-percent corporate tax paid in 12 downstate counties, also likely will see this measure extended.

Whether the lawmakers will give themselves pay hikes, raising their base pay from $57,500, remains a widely discussed rumor. While Bruno has said he would be surprised if a salary increase were enacted, he has admitted he at times has been surprised by political developments in Albany.

The budget reform proposals being considered include imposing a so-called austerity budget if a new pact were not approved on time, penalizing lawmakers by witholding their salaries, or extending the deadline, Bruno's spokesman said.
Under the proposals for an austerity budget, the previous budget would be cut by 10 percent and remain in effect until a new one was approved.

Gov. George Pataki, a Republican whose administration was harshly criticized for failing to get its 1997 fiscal budget approved until more than three months after it was due, has said he would like to have a contingency plan in place now, noting the state's budget has been late for 12 years in a row.

State budget director Patricia Woodworth has said she favors including some sort of punitive measure to force the Senate and the Assembly to agree on a budget on time, but she has reacted coolly when asked if changing the state's fiscal year would help improve the process.
"I don't think it would help but I might be surprised," she said on Monday at a Bond Buyer conference on New York.
